newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore-Malaysia row would not hurt trade.
newsitem.headline: Singapore-Malaysia row would not hurt trade.

text.p: Any serious row with neighbouring Malaysia was unlikely to damage trade-dependent Singapore's long-term links, analysts said on Thursday.
They said Malaysia had a history of using its increasing economic clout to punish countries which delivered perceived slights.
However, the analysts said any such row would have an impact in the short term.

They were commenting on reports by Malaysia's national news agency Bernama and Malaysian newspapers quoting unidentified ministers as saying after a cabinet meeting Wednesday that fresh initiatives with Singapore would be suspended, including new contracts to Singaporean companies.
Malaysia on Thursday denied it had frozen ties.

The sudden flare-up in relations came after remarks a month ago by Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew about the Malaysian state of Johor, which he said was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

Malaysia said on Thursday no decision had been made to freeze ties. Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said during a visit to Japan he was not sure what his cabinet had decided, but it was not "a major problem".

Economist Song Seng Wun of ABN/Amro Hoare Govett said Kuala Lumpur's past disputes with the Phillipines, Britain and Australia were eventually patched up after efforts were made by the offending countries to regain favour.
Malaysia did these things simply "to drive the point home", he said.
Nevertheless, there was no question that Malaysia was incensed by Lee's comment that its southern state of Johor
Even when accepting Lee's "unreserved apology", Malaysia said it would take time for the wound to heal.
But however deep the resentments, Singapore analysts said both countries had too much at stake in trade and investments to risk jeopardizing a long-term mutually beneficial relationship.

"There will always be people who can offer alternatives, but it's a matter of cost effectiveness. Malaysia is pragmatic enough not to cut off that benefit," said Andy Tan, an economist at MMS Standard and Poor's.
But a Malaysian clampdown on new business with Singapore could hurt Singapore's attempts to get a slice of Malaysia's numerous high-technology and developmental projects.
Mahathir's pet Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC) project, the Putrajaya development outside Kuala Lumpur and the Bakun Dam in Sarawak were among them, the analysts said.
"Singapore banks enjoy high earnings from Malaysian business because of strong loan demand," H.G. Asia's Song said.

Singapore's electronic companies have contracts in Malaysia, and are bidding for new ones. Being put at the end of the queue, where other countries deemed to have insulted Malaysia have been placed, would hurt.
The economists said many private projects in Malaysia were still government-linked.
Malaysia is Singapore's third largest trade partner after the United States and the European Community.
Singapore imported Singapore $2.4 billion (US$1.7 billion) worth of goods from Malaysia in December alone. Malaysia imported goods worth S$1.3 billion from Singapore in that month.
"The trade deficit is in Malaysia's favour," MMS's Tan said, noting this was one reason Malaysia would not prolong any spat.
But one analyst, who asked not to be identified, said it could be that the old ties were loosening.
"We are beginning to see a situation where both countries are looking beyond each other, even if it's less efficient and not cost effective," he said.
"The automatically high comfort levels shared by these two countries have been reduced. That has monetary value but cannot be put in dollar terms," he said.
